title: Approximating f -Divergences with Rank Statistics
claim: Matching distributions interleave samples to give a flat rank histogram; mismatched ones cluster in rank bins, and the non-uniformity measures divergence.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, samples on a line above rank histogram, blue vs red
description: Two rounded panels sit side by side. Panel (a), titled 'Ideal Case: μ = ν' in blue, has a horizontal 'Space X' axis. Filled dark-blue dots (μ) and hollow cyan circles (ν) alternate evenly along it. Dashed cyan vertical lines drop from the axis to a histogram with a 'Freq' y-axis and a 'Rank' x-axis. Six equal blue bars are labeled 'Uniform Histogram'. Panel (b), titled 'Mismatch: μ ≠ ν' in red, has the same layout. The μ dots bunch in the middle between a few spread-out ν circles. Only two tall red bars appear, in the central rank bins, and the outer bins are empty. A dashed horizontal line marks the uniform level, and a red 'High Divergence' label sits above the bars. Blue versus red draws the eye first.
caption: Conceptual illustration of the rank-statistic f-divergence. (a) When µ = ν, samples are uniformly interleaved, resulting in a uniform rank histogram. (b) With a mismatch, samples from µ cluster in specific rank bins, creating a non-uniform histogram that indicates divergence.
abstract: We introduce a rank-statistic approximation of $f$-divergences that avoids explicit density-ratio estimation by working directly with the distribution of ranks. For a resolution parameter $K$, we map the mismatch between two univariate distributions $Î¼$ and $Î½$ to a rank histogram on $\{ 0, \ldots, K\}$ and measure its deviation from uniformity via a discrete $f$-divergence, yielding a rank-statistic divergence estimator. We prove that the resulting estimator of the divergence is monotone in $K$, is always a lower bound of the true $f$-divergence, and we establish quantitative convergence rates for $K\to\infty$ under mild regularity of the quantile-domain density ratio. To handle high-dimensional data, we define the sliced rank-statistic $f$-divergence by averaging the univariate construction over random projections, and we provide convergence results for the sliced limit as well. We also derive finite-sample deviation bounds along with asymptotic normality results for the estimator. Finally, we empirically validate the approach by benchmarking against neural baselines and illustrating its use as a learning objective in generative modeling experiments.
